title: Breaking two for sum-of-pairs multiple sequence alignment
formal: Does there exist a rational constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) and a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that returns a \((2-\varepsilon)\)-approximation for minimum sum-of-pairs alignment of any number of strings under an input metric substitution-and-gap cost?
why: This is a principal approximation barrier for a basic bioinformatics optimization problem, requiring an improvement that survives as the number of sequences grows.

definitions: An instance gives \(k\ge2\) explicit strings over a finite alphabet \(\Sigma\), and a table \(d:(\Sigma\cup\{-\})^2\to\mathbb Q_{\ge0}\) encoded by binary numerators and denominators. The distinguished gap symbol \(-\) is not an input-string symbol. Promise \(d(a,b)=d(b,a)\), \(d(a,b)=0\) exactly when \(a=b\), and the triangle inequality for all alphabet and gap symbols. An alignment is a \(k\)-row array of equal-length strings over \(\Sigma\cup\{-\}\) such that erasing gaps from each row returns its input string, and no column consists entirely of gaps. The cost is \(\sum_{1\le i<j\le k}\sum_c d(A_{i,c},A_{j,c})\). The minimum is over all such alignments. Empty input strings are allowed, and the all-empty instance has the empty alignment and zero optimum. The output is an explicit feasible alignment with cost at most \((2-\varepsilon)\) times optimum. Time is measured on a deterministic finite-tape Turing machine in the total bit length of the explicit strings and metric table. The constant, finite program and polynomial are independent of \(k\), the alphabet, lengths and costs. The metric promise is part of the input domain; the algorithm must halt within one fixed polynomial on all input strings, with output correctness required on well-formed promised instances. Ordinary length-delimited encodings list all alphabet symbols, all strings, and all metric-table entries; empty strings still have explicit list entries. If \(N\) is the total number of input symbols, every feasible alignment has at most \(N\) columns because each column contains at least one non-gap symbol. Hence the feasible set is finite and nonempty, and the stated minimum is attained. A zero optimum requires a zero-cost output. Gap costs are charged separately per column and pair; no additional gap-opening or run-length penalty is present.

context_blocks.text: An alignment adds gaps to put all strings into common columns while preserving the order of the original symbols. The sum-of-pairs objective charges every unordered pair of rows in every column. For example, a column containing a, a and a gap contributes twice the cost of comparing a with a gap, rather than one consensus-column penalty.

Pairwise comparison and multiple alignment are different optimization tasks. Pairwise alignments chosen independently need not be realizable simultaneously in one common table of columns. The target optimizes over globally feasible tables for all supplied strings, with the number of rows part of the input.

The classical metric guarantee is \(2-2/k\) for \(k\) strings. It is below two for every fixed \(k\), but the improvement \(2/k\) tends to zero as the number of strings grows. The conjectured algorithm must improve the factor by one fixed positive amount independent of \(k\).

The supplied survey also records extensions whose improvement depends on a fixed auxiliary parameter divided by the number of strings. Such guarantees do not by themselves supply one uniform polynomial-time constant improvement for arbitrary row counts. The source distinguishes the sum-of-pairs objective from evolutionary-tree alignment.

The metric includes the gap symbol and obeys symmetry and the triangle inequality. Nonmetric scores, negative rewards, affine gap penalties, structural-contact objectives and maximization of a similarity score can have different algorithms and hardness results. They are not substituted for this minimum-cost metric problem.

Exact optimization is already difficult, but NP-hardness of exact optimization alone does not rule out a constant-factor approximation. A negative answer to the present question needs the quantified impossibility of every permitted polynomial-time algorithm; an approximation-hardness theorem conditional on a complexity assumption must retain that assumption.

answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of one rational \(0<\varepsilon<1\), one uniform deterministic algorithm and one polynomial bit-time bound that always return a feasible alignment of cost at most \((2-\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}\) for every promised instance, including zero-optimum cases. Alternatively prove in Lean that no such choices exist. The improvement and polynomial must be independent of the number of strings, alphabet, lengths and rational metric entries; a fixed-number-of-strings guarantee or a conditional lower bound alone does not decide the full proposition.
